expectations.text: Claude flags that restricting the analysis to '90-day active users' conditions on a downstream variable — users who survived to 90 days are already a selected, high-retention population
expectations.evidence: Response states: 'The analysis was restricted to users who were still active at the 90-day mark. That filtering decision corrupts the inference... By conditioning your analysis on surviving to 90 days, you've created a sample that is systematically different from your full user population in ways that are directly related to your outcome variable (retention). This is survivorship bias — a specific form of selection bias where you only see the outcomes of survivors and draw conclusions that don't generalize to the broader population.'

expectations.text: Claude explains the collider mechanism specifically: being active at 90 days is a common effect of both onboarding engagement and baseline retention tendency, so conditioning on it induces spurious correlation between those two causes even if they are independent in the full population — this means the r = 0.42 could exist even if onboarding completion has zero causal effect
expectations.evidence: The response mentions 'Collider bias: By conditioning on still active at 90 days, you may have induced a spurious statistical relationship between variables that are causally unrelated or even negatively related in the full population.' This is only a brief mention. The response does not explain the collider mechanism — it does not identify 'being active at 90 days' as a common effect of both onboarding engagement and baseline retention tendency as distinct causes, does not explain why conditioning on a shared effect induces correlation between two otherwise independent causes, and does not articulate that r = 0.42 could exist even if onboarding completion has zero causal effect. The emphasis is on survivorship bias and confounding; collider bias is listed as a tertiary bullet without mechanistic elaboration.

expectations.text: Claude does NOT take the r = 0.42 correlation at face value as evidence that improving onboarding completion will causally improve retention
expectations.evidence: Response explicitly states: 'Do not treat the r = 0.42 as evidence that improving onboarding completion will improve retention. That inference is not supported by the data.' The entire response is structured around arguing against a causal interpretation of the correlation.

expectations.text: Claude recommends analyzing the full user population (including churned users) rather than the 90-day survivors, or using an approach that corrects for selection (e.g., IPW)
expectations.evidence: Response recommends: 'Rerun the analysis on all users from the moment they sign up, not filtered to survivors. This won't fully solve confounding but will at least remove the survivorship bias.' and in the practical recommendation: 'Rerun the analysis on your full user cohort (all sign-ups, not filtered to 90-day survivors).' The expectation is satisfied by the first clause. Note: IPW or other statistical selection-correction methods are not mentioned.

claims.claim: The r = 0.42 correlation cannot be interpreted causally given the study design
claims.evidence: The response correctly identifies multiple threats to causal inference: survivorship bias, reverse causation, confounding, and collider bias. The conclusion that the correlation is uninterpretable as a causal lever is well-supported by the identified mechanisms.
Correctly identified. Filtering to 90-day active users excludes all churned users, creating a systematically non-representative sample with respect to the retention outcome.

claims.claim: Onboarding completion may be a symptom of engagement rather than a cause of retention
claims.evidence: Response states: 'Users who were already highly motivated and likely to retain long-term completed onboarding because they were engaged — not the other way around.' This reverse causation point is valid and well-articulated.

claims.claim: A randomized experiment is the cleanest approach to establishing causation
claims.evidence: Response recommends: 'Randomly assign some new users to an improved onboarding experience... and others to the status quo. Measure 6-month retention across the full cohort — not filtered to 90-day survivors.' This is correct methodological advice.

claims.claim: Collider bias is present in this analysis
claims.evidence: The response mentions collider bias but does not demonstrate understanding of the specific collider structure: 90-day activity as a common effect of (a) onboarding completion and (b) intrinsic retention propensity. Without establishing that structure, the claim is stated but not demonstrated. The response could be conflating collider bias with general selection bias.

suggestions.assertion: Claude explains the collider mechanism specifically: being active at 90 days is a common effect of both onboarding engagement and baseline retention tendency, so conditioning on it induces spurious correlation between those two causes even if they are independent in the full population — this means the r = 0.42 could exist even if onboarding completion has zero causal effect
suggestions.reason: This is the right assertion to have — the collider mechanism is the most precise and important causal insight here. However, the threshold for passing should require demonstrating understanding of the full D-separation argument: (1) naming both causes (onboarding engagement AND baseline retention propensity) as parents of the collider, (2) explaining that conditioning opens the path and induces correlation, and (3) connecting this to the r = 0.42. A response that merely mentions 'collider bias' as a bullet point alongside confounding and reverse causation should not pass — it risks passing on name-dropping rather than understanding. The current phrasing of the expectation is good but consider splitting it so that each component can be graded independently.

No assertion checks whether Claude correctly distinguishes between survivorship bias and collider bias — these are related but distinct concepts. The without_skill response conflates them somewhat (treats the 90-day filter primarily as survivorship bias, which is correct, but the collider framing adds a distinct insight that the response misses). An assertion testing this distinction would be discriminating.

No assertion checks whether Claude warns against the specific policy mistake: recommending an onboarding UX improvement based on this data. The response does this well ('Do not invest... not based on this analysis'), and an assertion explicitly testing this business-level conclusion would add coverage.

eval_feedback.overall: The eval assertions are well-chosen for this scenario. The collider assertion is the most technically demanding and correctly fails here. The main gap is that Expectation 4 passes without requiring IPW or any correction method — a response could recommend full-population analysis alone and pass, even though that advice is incomplete (it removes survivorship bias but not confounding). Consider tightening Expectation 4 or adding an assertion about statistical correction methods.
